title: Liverpool vs. Man City: Everything That Happened Off the Pitch in Gripping Psychodrama
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom1:28 PM EDTManchester City fans were defiant in the face of fierce opposition. / Peter Byrne/PA Images/Getty ImagesManchester City’s trip to Liverpool on Sunday could never be about the on-pitch action.

As soon as the Premier League dropped its explosive statement revealing how an independent commission had found City guilty of concocting “sham contracts,” “sham agreements” and “sham commercial deals” over nine seasons during the international break, the club’s next away game was always going to be hostile.

The fact their hosts would be Liverpool, a team with a fearsome and vocal fanbase enraged as direct victims of City’s “disguised funding scheme,” cranked up the anticipation of the occasion even more.

City would reestablish a three-point lead at the Premier League summit, Ryan Gravenberch skirted between hero and villain while Rayan Cherki delivered a contender for the most impish goal of the season. But plenty of focus was rightly directed away from the rectangle of green.

Circumstance meant that Merseyside on a sunny Sunday afternoon was never going to be mistaken for the seventh circle of hell, but Liverpool’s fans made sure there was the smell of sulfur in a red sky pregame.

Manchester City have had their run-ins with Liverpool’s fanbase on previous occasions. Bottles, cans and fireworks were infamously aimed at the club’s team bus ahead of a Champions League tie in 2018.
In order to avoid a repeat—or an escalation—of those scenes, City’s coach was steered to a second Anfield entrance away from the largest concentration of Liverpool fans.
City’s supporters weren’t kept quite as far away from their red counterparts, with some jostling and an exchange of jibes (rather than jabs) as police managed to contain the animosity.

There were tense scenes as a large group of City fans were escorted into the away end a few minutes ago. There were a couple of minor scuffles with stewards and some beer was thrown but other than that order was maintained pic.twitter.com/tGWKyjtd96

The fans who were not distracted by the prospect of a fight had the chance to mark this memorable occasion with a souvenir. The streets leading up to the stadium were lined with stalls teeming with pieces of memorabilia at City’s expense.

Some Liverpool fans were trying to cash in. / Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesThere was an Oasis flavor to a lot of the apparel, given the band’s famous support of City. Some of the visiting fans were inclined to make a few purchases of their own.
‘Guilty’ flags and ‘cheats’ scarves are among the merch being sold outside Anfield today pic.twitter.com/BfL57K1eYo
Liverpool fans boo the City players, the City fans boo the PL anthem. ‘We know what you are’ from the Kop, a Poznan in the away end. It’s had the lot! pic.twitter.com/NF3tfmY2DD

If there had been any doubt about the position of Liverpool’s supporters in regards to Manchester City’s guilt, they let it be known on Sunday. While most Premier League managers danced around the topic, Anfield was awash with flags and banners that spelled out the fans’ indignation in giant letters.
Liverpool had come prepared. / Peter Byrne/PA Images/Getty ImagesThe Kop has a banner with 114 pound signs (probably, I didn’t count) pic.twitter.com/Lba6P9Pka5

Man City’s owner come under fire. / Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesConsidering the limited goal threat from both sides across a scrappy opening 45 minutes, there was more creativity in the stands than on the pitch.

Liverpool fans got creative. / Peter Byrne/PA Images/Getty ImagesThere was more creativity in the stands than on the pitch. / Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesBanner in the Kop: ‘After All You Really Robbed Us All.’ pic.twitter.com/n2u5N20AXi

Ferran Soriano faced the music. / Michael Regan/Getty ImagesCity have taken a front-foot approach throughout these proceedings. The club still vehemently insist their innocence and chief executive Ferran Soriano was in the Anfield stands as a show of defiance.
Those above Soriano in City’s hierarchy didn’t brave the wall of noise, although chants and masks of the club’s owner Sheikh Mansour were prevalent on Merseyside.
